items.q: Which statement describes the greenhouse effect?
options: Low-level gases absorb infrared from the surface
Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs ultraviolet light from the Sun
Chlorine from CFCs destroys ozone and lets more UV reach the ground
Clouds reflect sunlight back to space and cool the planet

why.correct: The greenhouse effect: sunlight warms the surface, the surface gives off infrared, and greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit it, warming the lower atmosphere.
options: Right: greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared and send part of it back down.
That is the ozone layer’s job, a different process in a different layer.
That is ozone depletion, not the greenhouse effect.
Reflecting sunlight is part of albedo; the greenhouse effect traps outgoing infrared.

items.q: Without any greenhouse effect, Earth’s average surface temperature would be about −18 °C instead of about 15 °C. What does this show?
options: The greenhouse effect began with the Industrial Revolution
The natural effect keeps Earth warm enough for life
Earth would be warmer without greenhouse gases
Greenhouse gases block sunlight from reaching the surface

why.correct: The greenhouse effect is natural and necessary; the problem is the enhanced effect from added gases.
options: The natural effect existed long before people; humans are strengthening it.
Right: natural greenhouse gases warm the surface by about 33 °C.
Without them it would be about 33 °C colder.
Most sunlight passes through; the gases absorb outgoing infrared.

items.q: Which gas is NOT a greenhouse gas?
options: Methane (CH₄)
Nitrous oxide (N₂O)
Sulfur dioxide (SO₂)
Water vapor (H₂O)

why.correct: The main greenhouse gases are water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and CFCs. SO₂ and particulates are not greenhouse gases.
options: Methane absorbs infrared strongly; it is a greenhouse gas.
Nitrous oxide is a long-lived greenhouse gas.
Right: sulfur dioxide causes acid rain and forms particles that reflect sunlight; it is not a greenhouse gas.
Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas.

items.q: Which gas contributes the most to the natural greenhouse effect?
options: Ozone
Nitrogen gas
Oxygen gas
Water vapor

why.correct: Water vapor contributes the most, but the amount in the air depends on temperature; CO₂ and other gases set the temperature that water vapor then amplifies.
options: Ozone absorbs some infrared, but it is a small part of the greenhouse effect.
Nitrogen (N₂) is most of the air but does not absorb infrared.
Oxygen (O₂) does not absorb infrared, so it is not a greenhouse gas.
Right: water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas and causes most of the natural effect.

items.q: In the left panel, what kind of radiation do greenhouse gases absorb?
options: Infrared given off by Earth’s surface
Ultraviolet coming in from the Sun
Visible light coming in from the Sun
Radio waves from space

why.correct: Incoming sunlight is mostly visible light; outgoing radiation from the surface is infrared.
options: Right: the warm surface gives off infrared, which the gases absorb.
UV is absorbed by ozone in the stratosphere (right panel).
Most visible light passes through the atmosphere and warms the surface.
Radio waves are not part of either process in the figure.

items.q: According to the figure, which statement correctly contrasts the two processes?
options: Both processes take place in the stratosphere
Gases warm low air; ozone blocks UV high up
Both processes involve ultraviolet light from the Sun
Ozone traps infrared, and greenhouse gases absorb UV

why.correct: Two separate stories: infrared and the troposphere for warming, UV and the stratosphere for the ozone layer.
options: The greenhouse effect warms the troposphere, the lowest layer.
Right: different gases, radiation and layers.
The greenhouse effect involves outgoing infrared.
This swaps the two: ozone absorbs UV; greenhouse gases absorb infrared.

items.q: A student says, "The ozone hole lets more heat in, and that is what causes global warming." Using the figure, why is this wrong?
options: The ozone hole makes Earth colder, which cancels global warming
Global warming is caused by UV, so the student is right
The hole admits UV; warming is trapped infrared
The ozone hole is over the equator, where there is no warming

why.correct: Ozone depletion raises UV at the surface; the greenhouse effect traps infrared. Mixing them up is a common exam error.
options: Ozone loss is not a main cause of cooling or warming.
Warming is from trapped infrared, not UV.
Right: they involve different radiation and different gases.
The ozone hole is over Antarctica, and warming is global.

items.q: CFCs appear in both panels of the figure. Why?
options: CFCs are made of ozone, so they act like the ozone layer
CFCs absorb UV, which warms the lower atmosphere
The figure is wrong: CFCs belong in the right panel alone
CFCs trap infrared and also destroy ozone

why.correct: CFCs are the link between the two topics: they deplete ozone and trap heat. Carbon dioxide traps heat but does not deplete ozone.
options: CFCs contain chlorine, fluorine and carbon, not ozone.
CFCs warm the climate by absorbing infrared.
CFCs are strong greenhouse gases too.
Right: CFCs are both greenhouse gases and ozone-depleting substances.

items.q: A landfill releases 2.0 metric tons of methane in a year. Use the global warming potential of methane in the table, 28. What is this release in metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (the mass of CO₂ that would trap the same heat over 100 years)?

why.correct: $2.0\,\text{metric tons} \times 28 = 56$ metric tons of CO₂ equivalent.

mistakes.why: You divided by the global warming potential. Multiply: each ton of methane counts as 28 tons of CO₂, so 2.0 × 28.
265 is the global warming potential of nitrous oxide. Methane’s is 28.

items.q: A farm’s fertilized fields release 0.40 metric tons of nitrous oxide in a year. Use the global warming potential of nitrous oxide in the table, 265. Write the setup for the carbon dioxide equivalent, then give the answer in metric tons.

mistakes.why: Multiply by the global warming potential: each ton of N₂O counts as 265 tons of CO₂.
28 is methane’s global warming potential. Nitrous oxide’s is 265.
0.40 metric tons is the mass of N₂O. Multiply by 265 for the CO₂ equivalent: 106 metric tons.

items.q: One metric ton of which gas in the table traps the most heat over 100 years?
options: Carbon dioxide
Methane
CFC-12
Nitrous oxide

why.correct: Global warming potential compares the heat trapped by equal masses over 100 years, relative to CO₂.
options: CO₂ is the reference, with a global warming potential of 1, the smallest.
Methane’s 28 is far below CFC-12’s 10,200.
Right: its global warming potential, 10,200, is the largest in the table.
Nitrous oxide’s 265 is far below CFC-12’s 10,200.

items.q: CO₂ has the lowest global warming potential in the table, yet it causes the most human-made warming. Why?
options: CO₂ breaks down faster than the other gases
CO₂ also destroys ozone, which adds to the warming
The table is wrong: CO₂ has the highest potential
People release far more of it

why.correct: Total warming = amount released × potential. CO₂ is released in by far the largest amounts.
options: CO₂ stays in the air for centuries; the table’s other gases are not more short-lived in a way that explains this.
CO₂ does not destroy ozone.
CO₂ is the reference gas, set at 1 by definition.
Right: tens of billions of tons of CO₂ a year outweigh the much smaller releases of stronger gases.

items.q: Explain how adding carbon dioxide to the atmosphere warms Earth’s surface.

why.correct: Each link: more gas, more infrared absorbed, more re-emitted downward, less heat escapes, warmer surface.

specific.frame: More CO₂ ___ more of the ___ given off by the surface, so ___ is sent back down and surface temperature ___.

verb.label: What CO₂ does
options: absorbs
reflects
destroys

why.1: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared; they do not reflect it like a mirror.
why.2: CO₂ does not destroy radiation or ozone.

rad.label: Radiation
options: infrared radiation
ultraviolet radiation
visible light

why.1: UV comes from the Sun and is absorbed by ozone; the surface gives off infrared.
why.2: The surface gives off infrared, not visible light.

back.label: What is sent back
options: more heat
less heat

why.1: More absorbing gas sends more energy back toward the surface.

direction.label: Surface temperature
options: increases
decreases

why.1: Trapping more heat warms the surface.

specific.model: More CO₂ absorbs more of the infrared radiation given off by the surface and re-emits part of it toward the ground, so more heat is sent back down and the surface temperature increases because less heat escapes to space.

items.q: Which are greenhouse gases? Select all that apply.
options: Nitrogen gas (N₂)
Methane
Particulate matter
Sulfur dioxide

why.correct: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared: water vapor, CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide, CFCs and HFCs. Only methane is in this list.
options: Nitrogen is most of the air, but N₂ barely absorbs infrared, so it is not a greenhouse gas.
Right: methane is a strong greenhouse gas.
Particles are not gases; most reflect sunlight rather than trap infrared.
Sulfur dioxide is an acid-rain gas, not a greenhouse gas.

items.q: Why do nitrogen and oxygen, which make up 99% of dry air, not act as greenhouse gases?
options: They are found mostly high in the stratosphere
They absorb ultraviolet light instead of visible light
Their molecules hardly absorb infrared
They are produced by plants, so they do not trap heat

why.correct: A gas is a greenhouse gas only if its molecules absorb infrared; molecules of three or more atoms (CO₂, H₂O, CH₄, N₂O) do.
options: They fill the whole lower atmosphere.
That is not the reason; the point is that they do not absorb infrared.
Right: N₂ and O₂ molecules do not absorb infrared the way CO₂, CH₄ and H₂O do.
Where a gas comes from does not decide whether it absorbs infrared.
